title: Did Tom Platz know how to train LEGS? (Analyzing the Quadfather's Training Methods)
summary: NH critically analyses Tom Platz's leg training for natural lifters. Squats really are the best overall leg builder and build mental toughness, and Widowmaker 20-rep squats work. But Platz's ultra-intense, low-frequency, beyond-failure approach is unsustainable and injury-prone for naturals, who should spread volume, use Widowmakers sparingly and favor longevity.
claims: Don't blindly copy golden-era icons because of their charisma; judge their methods as if they came from a random guy
Any squat pattern (high bar, front, hack) is the king of lower-body exercises; there is no better overall stimulus for the legs and posterior chain
The gap between leg press and squat is minor; the leg press still builds big legs
If you love a lift and it works, stick with it rather than switching to something marginally more optimal
He built his big legs with squats alone
The squat triggers a life-or-death fight-or-flight response with the bar on your back that builds mental strength carrying over to life
Widowmaker squats: take a 10-rep-max weight and grind out 20 reps, resting with the bar racked on your back but never re-racking; the extra reps are high quality and it builds huge legs
Platz also squatted 225 lb continuously for 10 minutes and did 20-40 rep sets to failure
Ultra-taxing sessions force very low frequency; naturals should pick approaches that let them train legs as often as possible
The best method for any muscle is the one you can stick to longest; few people can run Widowmakers for a year
Beyond-failure reps aren't magic; the same work spread across the week gives more frequency, less soreness and better results
Use the Widowmaker squat as a single session plugged into the month, followed by time to flush fatigue, rather than as a whole cycle

Naturals have a muscle protein synthesis window of about 48-72 hours after training, while PED users stay anabolic around the clock, so naturals waste much of a week of recovery after one brutal session
Platz reportedly squatted only twice a month at one point
Squats stress the whole system and nervous system too, so the system, not the legs, can limit how soon you can train again
Always going all-out raises injury risk: Platz wrecked his shoulders, tore his bicep and had to retire
Accepting slightly fewer gains for longevity is always worth it; choose a method giving 70% of the gains for 10 years over 120% for two
Platz was built to squat; long-legged lifters who turn high-bar squats into good mornings should pick a variation that suits their leverages (e.g. hack squat)
Copying Platz's leg extension form would wreck most people's knees, and his sets of 60 leg curls would leave naturals too sore to walk
Soreness is not correlated with muscle growth
Avoiding squats because they are too hard is a mistake; there are safe ways to squat
Stop short of failure sometimes; like jiu-jitsu black belts who mostly flow-roll, don't go 100% every session
He once squatted three times a week with the same style and hit injuries and plateaus; treat the squat as a special lift and fill volume with leg press, leg extensions and hack squats
The squat is more axially loading than the deadlift, so spamming it makes the lower back the limiting factor
Hard work without smart work leads to destruction; the best natural physiques come from balancing safety and risk
exercises: high bar, front, hack all count; pick the variation that suits your leverages
best overall leg and posterior chain stimulus plus mental toughness
10RM load for 20 reps, rest-pause with bar on back, never re-rack
very effective but extremely taxing; use about once a month
only slightly inferior to squats; good accessory volume that spares the lower back
